{{Short description|Function used in optimal control theory}}
The '''Hamiltonian''' is a [[Function (mathematics)|function]] used to solve a problem of [[optimal control]] for a [[dynamical system]]. It can be understood as an instantaneous increment of the [[Lagrange multiplier|Lagrangian expression]] of the problem that is to be optimized over a certain time period.<ref>{{cite book |first1=Brian S. |last1=Ferguson |first2=G. C. |last2=Lim |title=Introduction to Dynamic Economic Problems |location=Manchester |publisher=Manchester University Press |year=1998 |isbn=0-7190-4996-2 |pages=166–167 }}</ref> Inspired by—but distinct from—the [[Hamiltonian mechanics|Hamiltonian of classical mechanics]], the Hamiltonian of optimal control theory was developed by [[Lev Pontryagin]] as part of his [[Pontryagin's minimum principle|maximum principle]].<ref>{{cite book |first=Avinash K. |last=Dixit |title=Optimization in Economic Theory |location=New York |publisher=Oxford University Press |year=1990 |isbn=978-0-19-877210-1 |pages=145–161 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=dHrsHz0VocUC&pg=PA145 }}</ref> Pontryagin proved that a necessary condition for solving the optimal control problem is that the control should be chosen so as to optimize the Hamiltonian.<ref>{{cite book |first=Donald E. |last=Kirk |title=Optimal Control Theory : An Introduction |location=Englewood Cliffs |publisher=Prentice Hall |year=1970 |isbn=0-13-638098-0 |page=232 }}</ref>

== Problem statement and definition of the Hamiltonian ==
Consider a [[dynamical system]] of <math>n</math> first-order [[differential equation]]s
:<math>\dot{\mathbf{x}}(t) = \mathbf{f}(\mathbf{x}(t),\mathbf{u}(t),t)</math>
where <math>\mathbf{x}(t) = \left[ x_{1}(t), x_{2}(t), \ldots, x_{n}(t) \right]^{\mathsf{T}}</math> denotes a vector of state variables, and <math>\mathbf{u}(t) = \left[ u_{1}(t), u_{2}(t), \ldots, u_{r}(t) \right]^{\mathsf{T}}</math> a vector of control variables. Once initial conditions <math>\mathbf{x}(t_{0}) = \mathbf{x}_{0}</math> and controls <math>\mathbf{u}(t)</math> are specified, a solution to the differential equations, called a ''trajectory'' <math>\mathbf{x}(t; \mathbf{x}_{0}, t_{0})</math>, can be found. The problem of optimal control is to choose <math>\mathbf{u}(t)</math> (from some set  <math>\mathcal{U} \subseteq \mathbb{R}^{r}</math>) so that <math>\mathbf{x}(t)</math> maximizes or minimizes a certain [[Loss function|objective function]] between an initial time <math>t = t_{0}</math> and a terminal time <math>t = t_{1}</math> (where <math>t_{1}</math> may be [[infinity]]). Specifically, the goal is to optimize over a performance index <math>I(\mathbf{x}(t),\mathbf{u}(t),t)</math> defined at each point in time,
:<math>\max_{\mathbf{u}(t)} J</math>, with <math>J = \int_{t_{0}}^{t_{1}} I[\mathbf{x}(t),\mathbf{u}(t),t] \, \mathrm{d}t</math>
subject to the above equations of motion of the state variables. The solution method involves defining an ancillary function known as the control Hamiltonian
{{Equation box 1
|indent =:
|equation = <math>H(\mathbf{x}(t),\mathbf{u}(t),\mathbf{\lambda}(t),t) \equiv I(\mathbf{x}(t),\mathbf{u}(t),t) + \mathbf{\lambda}^{\mathsf{T}}(t) \mathbf{f}(\mathbf{x}(t),\mathbf{u}(t),t)</math>
|cellpadding
|border
|border colour = #50C878
|background colour = #ECFCF4}}
which combines the objective function and the state equations much like a [[Lagrange multiplier|Lagrangian]] in a static optimization problem, only that the  multipliers <math>\mathbf{\lambda}(t)</math>—referred to as ''costate variables''—are functions of time rather than constants.

The goal is to find an optimal control policy function <math>\mathbf{u}^\ast(t)</math> and, with it, an optimal trajectory of the state variable <math>\mathbf{x}^\ast(t)</math>, which by [[Pontryagin's maximum principle]] are the arguments that maximize the Hamiltonian,
:<math>H(\mathbf{x}^\ast(t),\mathbf{u}^\ast(t),\mathbf{\lambda}(t),t) \geq H(\mathbf{x}(t),\mathbf{u}(t),\mathbf{\lambda}(t),t)</math> for all <math>\mathbf{u}(t) \in \mathcal{U}</math>
The first-order necessary conditions for a maximum are given by

:<math>\frac{\partial H(\mathbf{x}(t),\mathbf{u}(t),\mathbf{\lambda}(t),t)}{\partial \mathbf{u}} = 0 \quad</math> which is the maximum principle,
:<math>\frac{\partial H(\mathbf{x}(t),\mathbf{u}(t),\mathbf{\lambda}(t),t)}{\partial \mathbf{\lambda}} = \dot{\mathbf{x}}(t) \quad</math> which generates the state transition function <math>\, \mathbf{f}(\mathbf{x}(t),\mathbf{u}(t),t) = \dot{\mathbf{x}}(t)</math>,
:<math>\frac{\partial H(\mathbf{x}(t),\mathbf{u}(t),\mathbf{\lambda}(t),t)}{\partial \mathbf{x}} = - \dot{\mathbf{\lambda}}(t) \quad</math> which generates the [[costate equation]]s <math>\, \dot{\mathbf{\lambda}}(t) = - \left[ I_{\mathbf{x}}(\mathbf{x}(t),\mathbf{u}(t),t) + \mathbf{\lambda}^{\mathsf{T}}(t) \mathbf{f}_{\mathbf{x}}(\mathbf{x}(t),\mathbf{u}(t),t) \right]</math>

Together, the state and costate equations describe the Hamiltonian dynamical system (again analogous to but distinct from the [[Hamiltonian system]] in physics), the solution of which involves a two-point [[boundary value problem]], given that there are <math>2n</math> boundary conditions involving two different points in time, the initial time (the <math>n</math> differential equations for the state variables), and the terminal time (the <math>n</math> differential equations for the costate variables; unless a final function is specified, the boundary conditions are <math>\mathbf{\lambda}(t_{1}) = 0</math>, or <math>\lim_{t_{1} \to \infty} \mathbf{\lambda}(t_{1}) = 0</math> for infinite time horizons).<ref>{{cite book |first=Giancarlo |last=Gandolfo |title=Economic Dynamics |location=Berlin |publisher=Springer |edition=Third |year=1996 |isbn=3-540-60988-1 |pages=375–376 }}</ref>

A sufficient condition for a maximum is the concavity of the Hamiltonian evaluated at the solution, i.e.
:<math>H_{\mathbf{uu}}(\mathbf{x}^\ast(t),\mathbf{u}^\ast(t),\mathbf{\lambda}(t),t) \leq 0</math>
where <math>\mathbf{u}^\ast(t)</math> is the optimal control, and <math>\mathbf{x}^\ast(t)</math> is resulting optimal trajectory for the [[state variable]].<ref>{{cite book |first1=Atle |last1=Seierstad |first2=Knut |last2=Sydsæter |author-link2=Knut Sydsæter |title=Optimal Control Theory with Economic Applications |location=Amsterdam |publisher=North-Holland |year=1987 |pages=107–110 |isbn=0-444-87923-4 }}</ref> Alternatively, by a result due to [[Olvi L. Mangasarian]], the necessary conditions are sufficient if the functions <math>I(\mathbf{x}(t),\mathbf{u}(t),t)</math> and <math>\mathbf{f}(\mathbf{x}(t),\mathbf{u}(t),t)</math> are both concave in <math>\mathbf{x}(t)</math> and <math>\mathbf{u}(t)</math>.<ref>{{cite journal |journal=SIAM Journal on Control |volume=4 |year=1966 |issue=1 |pages=139–152 |title=Sufficient Conditions for the Optimal Control of Nonlinear Systems |first=O. L. |last=Mangasarian |doi=10.1137/0304013 }}</ref>

=== Derivation from the Lagrangian ===
A [[constrained optimization]] problem as the one stated above usually suggests a Lagrangian expression, specifically 
:<math>L = \int_{t_{0}}^{t_{1}} I(\mathbf{x}(t),\mathbf{u}(t),t) + \mathbf{\lambda}^{\mathsf{T}}(t) \left[ \mathbf{f}(\mathbf{x}(t),\mathbf{u}(t),t) - \dot{\mathbf{x}}(t) \right] \, \mathrm{d}t</math>
where <math>\mathbf{\lambda}(t)</math> compares to the [[Lagrange multiplier]] in a static optimization problem but is now, as noted above, a function of time. In order to eliminate <math>\dot{\mathbf{x}}(t)</math>, the last term on the right-hand side can be rewritten using [[integration by parts]], such that
:<math>- \int_{t_{0}}^{t_{1}} \mathbf{\lambda}^{\mathsf{T}}(t) \dot{\mathbf{x}}(t) \, \mathrm{d}t = -\mathbf{\lambda}^{\mathsf{T}}(t_{1}) \mathbf{x}(t_{1}) + \mathbf{\lambda}^{\mathsf{T}}(t_{0}) \mathbf{x}(t_{0}) + \int_{t_{0}}^{t_{1}} \dot{\mathbf{\lambda}}^{\mathsf{T}}(t) \mathbf{x}(t) \, \mathrm{d}t </math>
which can be substituted back into the Lagrangian expression to give
:<math>L = \int_{t_{0}}^{t_{1}} \left[ I(\mathbf{x}(t),\mathbf{u}(t),t) + \mathbf{\lambda}^{\mathsf{T}}(t) \mathbf{f}(\mathbf{x}(t),\mathbf{u}(t),t) + \dot{\mathbf{\lambda}}^{\mathsf{T}}(t) \mathbf{x}(t) \right] \, \mathrm{d}t - \mathbf{\lambda}^{\mathsf{T}}(t_{1}) \mathbf{x}(t_{1}) + \mathbf{\lambda}^{\mathsf{T}}(t_{0}) \mathbf{x}(t_{0}) </math>
To derive the first-order conditions for an optimum, assume that the solution has been found and the Lagrangian is maximized. Then any perturbation to <math>\mathbf{x}(t)</math> or <math>\mathbf{u}(t)</math> must cause the value of the Lagrangian to decline. Specifically, the [[total derivative]] of <math>L</math> obeys
:<math>\mathrm{d}L = \int_{t_{0}}^{t_{1}} \left[ \left( I_{\mathbf{u}}(\mathbf{x}(t),\mathbf{u}(t),t) + \mathbf{\lambda}^{\mathsf{T}}(t) \mathbf{f}_{\mathbf{u}}(\mathbf{x}(t),\mathbf{u}(t),t) \right) \mathrm{d}\mathbf{u}(t) + \left( I_{\mathbf{x}}(\mathbf{x}(t),\mathbf{u}(t),t) + \mathbf{\lambda}^{\mathsf{T}}(t) \mathbf{f}_{\mathbf{x}}(\mathbf{x}(t),\mathbf{u}(t),t) + \dot{\mathbf{\lambda}}(t) \right) \mathrm{d}\mathbf{x}(t) \right] \mathrm{d}t - \mathbf{\lambda}^{\mathsf{T}}(t_{1}) \mathrm{d}\mathbf{x}(t_{1}) + \mathbf{\lambda}^{\mathsf{T}}(t_{0}) \mathrm{d}\mathbf{x}(t_{0}) \leq 0</math>
For this expression to equal zero necessitates the following optimality conditions:
:<math>\begin{align}
\underbrace{I_{\mathbf{u}}(\mathbf{x}(t),\mathbf{u}(t),t) + \mathbf{\lambda}^{\mathsf{T}}(t) \mathbf{f}_{\mathbf{u}}(\mathbf{x}(t),\mathbf{u}(t),t)}_{= \frac{\partial H(\mathbf{x}(t),\mathbf{u}(t),\mathbf{\lambda}(t),t)}{\partial \mathbf{u}}} &= 0 \\
\underbrace{I_{\mathbf{x}}(\mathbf{x}(t),\mathbf{u}(t),t) + \mathbf{\lambda}^{\mathsf{T}}(t) \mathbf{f}_{\mathbf{x}}(\mathbf{x}(t),\mathbf{u}(t),t)}_{= \frac{\partial H(\mathbf{x}(t),\mathbf{u}(t),\mathbf{\lambda}(t),t)}{\partial \mathbf{x}}} + \dot{\mathbf{\lambda}}(t) &= 0
\end{align}</math>
If both the initial value <math>\mathbf{x}(t_{0})</math> and terminal value <math>\mathbf{x}(t_{1})</math> are fixed, i.e. <math>\mathrm{d}\mathbf{x}(t_{0}) = \mathrm{d}\mathbf{x}(t_{1}) = 0</math>, no conditions on <math>\mathbf{\lambda}(t_{0})</math> and <math>\mathbf{\lambda}(t_{1})</math> are needed. If the terminal value is free, as is often the case, the additional condition <math>\mathbf{\lambda}(t_{1}) = 0</math> is necessary for optimality. The latter is called a transversality condition for a fixed horizon problem.<ref>{{cite book |first1=Daniel |last1=Léonard |first2=Ngo Van |last2=Long |title=Optimal Control Theory and Static Optimization in Economics |location=New York |publisher=Cambridge University Press |year=1992 |chapter=Endpoint Constraints and Transversality Conditions |isbn=0-521-33158-7 |page=222 [Theorem 7.1.1] |chapter-url=https://books.google.com/books?id=gSHxK5Cq4BgC&pg=PA222 }}</ref>

It can be seen that the necessary conditions are identical to the ones stated above for the Hamiltonian. Thus the Hamiltonian can be understood as a device to generate the first-order necessary conditions.<ref>{{cite book |first1=Morton I. |last1=Kamien |first2=Nancy L. |last2=Schwartz |title=Dynamic Optimization : The Calculus of Variances and Optimal Control in Economics and Management |location=Amsterdam |publisher=North-Holland |edition=Second |year=1991 |isbn=0-444-01609-0 |pages=126–127 }}</ref>

== The Hamiltonian in discrete time ==

When the problem is formulated in discrete time, the Hamiltonian is defined as:

:<math>
H(x_{t},u_{t},\lambda_{t+1},t)=\lambda^\top_{t+1}f(x_{t},u_{t},t)+I(x_{t},u_{t},t) \,
</math>

and the [[costate equations]] are

:<math>
\lambda_{t} =\frac{\partial H}{\partial x_{t}}
</math>
(Note that the discrete time Hamiltonian at time <math>t</math> involves the costate variable at time <math>t+1.</math><ref>{{cite web |first=U. |last=Jönsson |title=A DISCRETE VERSION OF PMP |year=2005 |pages=25 |url=https://www.math.kth.se/optsyst/grundutbildning/5B1872/Discrete.pdf |archive-date=January 22, 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230122192015/https://www.math.kth.se/optsyst/grundutbildning/5B1872/Discrete.pdf }}</ref>  This small detail is essential so that when we differentiate with respect to <math>x</math> we get a term involving <math>\lambda_{t+1}</math> on the right hand side of the costate equations. Using a wrong convention here can lead to incorrect results, i.e. a costate equation which is not a backwards difference equation).

== Behavior of the Hamiltonian over time ==
From Pontryagin's maximum principle, special conditions for the Hamiltonian can be derived.<ref>{{cite book |first=Desineni S. |last=Naidu |title=Optimal Control Systems |location=Boca Raton |publisher=CRC Press |year=2003 |isbn=0-8493-0892-5 |pages=259–260 }}</ref> When the final time <math>t_1</math> is fixed and the Hamiltonian does not depend explicitly on time <math>\left(\tfrac{\partial H}{\partial t} = 0\right)</math>, then:<ref>{{cite journal |first=Delfim F. M. |last=Torres |title=A Remarkable Property of the Dynamic Optimization Extremals |journal=Investigacao Operacional |volume=22 |issue=2 |year=2002 |pages=253–263 |arxiv=math/0212102 |bibcode=2002math.....12102T }}</ref>
:<math>H(x^*(t),u^*(t),\lambda^*(t)) = \mathrm{constant}\,</math>
or if the terminal time is free, then:
:<math>H(x^*(t),u^*(t),\lambda^*(t)) = 0.\,</math>
Further, if the terminal time tends to [[infinity]], a [[transversality condition]] on the Hamiltonian applies.<ref>{{cite journal |first=Philippe |last=Michel |author-link=Philippe Michel (economist) |title=On the Transversality Condition in Infinite Horizon Optimal Problems |journal=[[Econometrica]] |volume=50 |issue=4 |year=1982 |pages=975–985 |doi=10.2307/1912772 |jstor=1912772 |s2cid=16503488 }}</ref>
:<math>\lim_{t \to \infty} H(t) = 0</math>

== The Hamiltonian of control compared to the Hamiltonian of mechanics ==

[[William Rowan Hamilton]] defined the [[Hamiltonian mechanics|Hamiltonian]] for describing the mechanics of a system. It is a function of three variables and related to the Lagrangian as

:<math>\mathcal{H}(p,q,t) = \langle p,\dot{q} \rangle -L(q,\dot{q},t)</math>

where <math>L</math> is the [[Lagrangian mechanics|Lagrangian]], the extremizing of which determines the dynamics (''not'' the Lagrangian defined above) and <math>q</math> is the state variable. The Lagrangian is evaluated with <math>\dot{q}</math> representing the [[time derivative]] of the state's evolution and <math>p</math>, the so-called "[[conjugate momentum]]", relates to it as

:<math>p = \frac{\partial L}{\partial \dot{q}}</math>.

Hamilton then formulated his equations to describe the dynamics of the system as

:<math>\frac{ d}{ dt}p(t) = -\frac{\partial}{\partial q}\mathcal{H}</math>
:<math>\frac{ d}{ dt}q(t) =~~\frac{\partial}{\partial p}\mathcal{H}</math>

The Hamiltonian of control theory describes not the ''dynamics'' of a system but conditions for extremizing some scalar function thereof (the Lagrangian) with respect to a control variable <math>u</math>. As normally defined, it is a function of 4 variables

:<math>H(q,u,p,t)= \langle p,\dot{q} \rangle -L(q,u,t)</math>

where <math>q</math> is the state variable and <math>u</math> is the control variable with respect to that which we are extremizing.

The associated conditions for a maximum are

:<math>\frac{dp}{dt} = -\frac{\partial H}{\partial q}</math>

:<math>\frac{dq}{dt} = ~~\frac{\partial H}{\partial p}</math>

:<math>\frac{\partial H}{\partial u} = 0</math>

This definition agrees with that given by the article by Sussmann and Willems.<ref>{{cite journal |url=http://yima.csl.illinois.edu/psfile/ECE553/sussmann-willems.pdf |last1=Sussmann |last2= Willems |title=300 Years of Optimal Control |journal=IEEE Control Systems Magazine |date=June 1997 |doi=10.1109/37.588098 |archive-date=July 30, 2010 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100730033612/http://yima.csl.illinois.edu/psfile/ECE553/sussmann-willems.pdf }}</ref> (see p.&nbsp;39, equation 14). Sussmann and Willems show how the control Hamiltonian can be used in dynamics e.g. for the [[brachistochrone problem]], but do not mention the prior work of [[Carathéodory]] on this approach.<ref>See {{cite journal |first1=H. J. |last1=Pesch |first2=R. |last2=Bulirsch |title=The maximum principle, Bellman's equation, and Carathéodory's work |journal=[[Journal of Optimization Theory and Applications]] |volume=80 |year=1994 |issue=2 |pages=199–225 |doi=10.1007/BF02192933 |s2cid=121749702 }}</ref>

== Current value and present value Hamiltonian ==
In [[economics]], the objective function in dynamic optimization problems often depends directly on time only through [[exponential discounting]], such that it takes the form
:<math>I(\mathbf{x}(t),\mathbf{u}(t),t) = e^{-\rho t} \nu(\mathbf{x}(t),\mathbf{u}(t))</math>
where <math>\nu(\mathbf{x}(t),\mathbf{u}(t))</math> is referred to as the instantaneous [[utility function]], or [[felicity function]].<ref>{{cite web |title=Econ 4350: Growth and Investment: Lecture Note 7 |publisher=Department of Economics, University of Oslo |first=Kåre |last=Bævre |date=Spring 2005 |url=https://www.uio.no/studier/emner/sv/oekonomi/ECON4350/v05/undervisningsmateriale/lecture_notes/4350_ln7.pdf#page=2 }}</ref> This allows a redefinition of the Hamiltonian as <math>H(\mathbf{x}(t),\mathbf{u}(t),\mathbf{\lambda}(t),t) = e^{-\rho t} \bar{H}(\mathbf{x}(t),\mathbf{u}(t),\mathbf{\lambda}(t))</math> where
:<math>\begin{align}
\bar{H}(\mathbf{x}(t),\mathbf{u}(t),\mathbf{\lambda}(t)) \equiv& \, e^{\rho t} \left[ I(\mathbf{x}(t),\mathbf{u}(t),t) + \mathbf{\lambda}^{\mathsf{T}}(t) \mathbf{f}(\mathbf{x}(t),\mathbf{u}(t),t) \right] \\
=& \, \nu(\mathbf{x}(t),\mathbf{u}(t),t) + \mathbf{\mu}^{\mathsf{T}}(t) \mathbf{f}(\mathbf{x}(t),\mathbf{u}(t),t)
\end{align}</math>
which is referred to as the current value Hamiltonian, in contrast to the present value Hamiltonian <math>H(\mathbf{x}(t),\mathbf{u}(t),\mathbf{\lambda}(t),t)</math> defined in the first section. Most notably the costate variables are redefined as <math>\mathbf{\mu}(t) = e^{\rho t} \mathbf{\lambda}(t)</math>, which leads to modified first-order conditions. 
:<math>\frac{\partial \bar{H}(\mathbf{x}(t),\mathbf{u}(t),\mathbf{\lambda}(t))}{\partial \mathbf{u}} = 0</math>,
:<math>\frac{\partial \bar{H}(\mathbf{x}(t),\mathbf{u}(t),\mathbf{\lambda}(t))}{\partial \mathbf{x}} = - \dot{\mathbf{\mu}}(t) + \rho \mathbf{\mu}(t)</math>
which follows immediately from the [[product rule]]. Economically, <math>\mathbf{\mu}(t)</math> represent current-valued [[shadow price]]s for the capital goods <math>\mathbf{x}(t)</math>.

== Example: Ramsey–Cass–Koopmans model ==
In [[economics]], the [[Ramsey–Cass–Koopmans model]] is used to determine an optimal savings behavior for an economy. The objective function <math>J(c)</math> is the [[social welfare function]],
:<math>J(c) = \int^T_0 e^{-\rho t}u(c(t)) dt</math>
to be maximized by choice of an optimal consumption path <math>c(t)</math>. The function <math>u(c(t))</math> indicates the [[utility]] the [[representative agent]] of consuming <math>c</math> at any given point in time. The factor <math>e^{-\rho t}</math> represents [[discounting]]. The maximization problem is subject to the following differential equation for [[capital intensity]], describing the [[time evolution]] of capital per effective worker:
:<math>\dot{k}=\frac{\partial k}{\partial t} =f(k(t)) - (n + \delta)k(t) - c(t)</math>
where <math>c(t)</math> is period t consumption, <math>k(t)</math> is period t capital per worker (with <math>k(0) = k_{0} > 0</math>), <math>f(k(t))</math> is period t production, <math>n</math> is the population growth rate, <math>\delta</math> is the capital depreciation rate, the agent discounts future utility at rate <math>\rho</math>, with <math>u'>0</math> and <math>u''<0</math>.

Here, <math>k(t)</math> is the state variable which evolves according to the above equation, and <math>c(t)</math> is the control variable. The Hamiltonian becomes

:<math>H(k,c,\mu,t)=e^{-\rho t}u(c(t))+\mu(t)\dot{k}=e^{-\rho t}u(c(t))+\mu(t)[f(k(t)) - (n + \delta)k(t) - c(t)]</math>

The optimality conditions are

:<math>\frac{\partial H}{\partial c}=0 \Rightarrow
e^{-\rho t}u'(c)=\mu(t)</math>
:<math>\frac{\partial H}{\partial k}=-\frac{\partial \mu}{\partial t}=-\dot{\mu} \Rightarrow \mu(t)[f'(k)-(n+\delta)]=-\dot{\mu}</math>

in addition to the transversality condition <math>\mu(T)k(T)=0</math>. If we let <math>u(c)=\log(c)</math>, then [[Logarithmic differentiation|log-differentiating]] the first optimality condition with respect to <math>t</math> yields

:<math>-\rho-\frac{\dot{c}}{c(t)}=\frac{\dot{\mu}}{\mu(t)}</math>

Inserting this equation into the second optimality condition yields

:<math>\rho+\frac{\dot{c}}{c(t)}=f'(k)-(n+\delta)</math>

which is known as the [[Keynes–Ramsey rule]], which gives a condition for consumption in every period which, if followed, ensures maximum lifetime utility.
